results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.quote: **Where we are in the order's journey.** Eva's €235 purchase on 13 April 2027 becomes order #1072455
results.finding: Declared 'example' carrying over 'definitions that decide what counts', placed at the start; the paragraph opens on a journey label and an unrelated April date, and the link to definitions arrives only in its last sentence. Both flow readers lost the thread here.

results.quote: Eva's €235 purchase on 13 April 2027 becomes order #1072455, invoice lines and a parcel dispatched on 14 April.
results.finding: Readers found the jump to April and to Eva's storyline, between the thesis and the roadmap, disconnected; nothing says the chapter returns to her order in In Practice.
results.corroborated_by: second flow reader (flowB), item 3, second bullet

results.quote: Daniel's report comes from a **business intelligence (BI)** tool reading the **warehouse management system (WMS)**.
results.finding: Only one of the three counts is given a source; readers had to infer from the table headers that Milan's is the platform's and Sanne's the ERP's, and why nobody reports from the data warehouse.
results.corroborated_by: second flow reader (flowB), item 3, third bullet

results.quote: The analytical store has had two names.
results.finding: 'Two names' signals synonyms, but the next paragraph presents the lakehouse as a different design that criticised the warehouse (declared relationship p14: contrast); readers re-read to reconcile.
results.corroborated_by: second flow reader (flowB), item 3, fourth bullet

results.draft_locus: The Choices and Their Trade-offs (design table) and Across Scale Stages (stage table)
results.quote: | Warehouse, ELT, metrics layer | ... | Two or more channels; Omnichannel stage; Kestrel & Pine from 2027 |
results.finding: Two mappings of design to stage: the design table puts the warehouse with ELT at Omnichannel and calls BI on copies 'never for a multi-channel merchant', while the stage table makes a warehouse with ELT necessary at Growing and BI on exports typical there; readers had to reconcile them (the AC-3 reader noticed it too).
results.corroborated_by: second flow reader (flowB), item 2 (Across Scale Stages) and item 4 first bullet

results.quote: The chapter began with two correct but different totals at one meeting.
results.finding: Readers take 'the meeting' as the March meeting, which had three counts; the callback to the introduction's finance-and-operations example is ambiguous and made both re-read.
results.corroborated_by: second flow reader (flowB), item 3, first bullet

results.draft_locus: One Definition: Metrics and the Metrics Layer ¶7
results.quote: the order domain (the OMS team after W2) owns the order dataset and its definitions
results.finding: Appears to contradict W7, which gives the order definition to the Data Lead; the tension is resolved only in the takeaways ('under about five data people, one owner'). Reported by one reader only.

results.quote: Whether definitions are owned centrally or by domains depends on team size: under about five data people, one owner (the Data Lead) with domain reviewers; beyond that, domain ownership with central standards
results.finding: The team-size rule is a new idea introduced in the conclusion: the body (p36) says only that ownership follows domains, so the conclusion resolves a body contradiction (domain ownership vs W7's Data Lead) with a criterion the body never states. The spec puts the dependence only in p53, not in p36.
